body: Concrete roads are extremely common in the Philippines. However, be aware that Thailand also has many concrete roads.
The Philippines drives on the right. This is similar to Cambodia, Laos, and Taiwan within Southeast Asia.
Standard passenger vehicles in the Philippines use white licence plates with black text. Privately issued plates are also common and can be recognized by their green tint.
Octagonal metal poles are common in the Philippines. Note that they can also be found in Bangladesh and parts of Malaysia.
A common sight on utility poles is a single insulator at the top of a vertical bar attached to the pole's side.
The Philippines often uses combined yellow and white middle road lines, a unique feature in East Asia. The yellow lines frequently have a distinct orange tint.
Tall, square yellow road stones are a unique feature of the Philippines.
Chevrons in the Philippines are typically red on a white background.
Signposts in the Philippines are often painted red, orange, or yellow.
Tuk-tuks, also known as tricycles, are extremely common throughout the Philippines, often outnumbering cars in many areas.
While Filipino is the official language, English is extremely common on signs, making it the only major Southeast Asian country where this is the case.
In Generation 3 coverage, you might see a white Street View car with a visible black roof. A silvery-grey car, also seen in Bhutan, may also appear.
It is common to see grains spread out on roads to dry. This practice is also common in Vietnam.
Black or white boxes on utility poles often display a three-letter abbreviation for the municipality. These abbreviations can help identify your location, though they are not always standardized.
The Philippines has several different tuk-tuk and tricycle designs that can help with region guessing. The designs are roughly distributed as shown in the infographic.
Province names are very common on signs and are useful for region-guessing if you memorize them, as they don't appear on the map.
Landline numbers start with a 0 followed by the area code, while mobile phone numbers start with 09.
Motorcycle licence plates are regionally color-coded. The colored strip is at the top in the northern half of the country and at the bottom in the southern half.
The mountain range in Northern Luzon is characterized by somewhat dry mountainsides and an abundance of pine trees. A similar landscape can rarely be found on high-altitude roads in Mindanao.
Corn is most commonly grown in northern Luzon and on the island of Mindanao.
The vast majority of oil palm plantations are found on the island of Mindanao.
Most of the Philippines' sugarcane is grown on the islands of Negros and Panay.
Pineapple plantations are mostly found on the island of Mindanao.
Banana plantations are found almost exclusively in central and southern Mindanao. Be careful not to confuse them with wild banana plants found throughout the country.
Moluccan albizia trees, with their light-colored trunks and pinnate leaves, are mainly found on Mindanao, especially in the eastern and central regions.
Houses with amakan walls (woven bamboo) featuring a diamond pattern are almost exclusively found in the southern half of the country.
Houses with amakan walls (called Sawali in the north) with a diagonally woven pattern are mostly found on Palawan, but can also be seen in the northern half of the country.
In the Cordillera Administrative Region, you can find distinctive yellow and black striped concrete guardrails.
White guardrails with three recurring black stripes are a unique feature of the Bicol region in southern Luzon.
Square concrete poles with an indent on both sides, similar to those in Chile, are mainly found north of Manila and around Bacolod on Negros island.
A unique 'ladder' poletop, made of two tall L-shaped vertical metal bars connected by several thin wires, is specific to Manila and its surrounding area.
Square metal mesh poles are primarily found on the Zamboanga peninsula in Mindanao. Outside this area, they usually have poletops with three hanging insulators along highways.
While most of the Philippines is Christian, the region of western Mindanao is majority Muslim.
Decorations made from neon-green Mountain Dew bottles are a common sight in the north, especially on northern Luzon.
The kuliglig, a type of tractor, is mostly found on the plains around Cauayan in northern Luzon.
The Chocolate Hills, located on central Bohol, are distinct round grassy hills with dark brown soil underneath.
The Arayat Volcano is recognizable by being an isolated mountain completely surrounded by flat agricultural fields.
The Mayon Volcano is one of the tallest mountains in the Philippines and is recognizable by its almost perfect, smooth cone shape, though it's often covered in clouds.
In and around Marawi, Mindanao, you can find many destroyed houses and ruins from the 2017 Marawi siege.
Large, decorated white waystones commemorating the Bataan Death March can be found along roads from Mariveles and Bagac to San Fernando.
The highway south of Puerto Princesa on Palawan is unusually wide with little traffic. A double electrical wire along the road is a good confirming clue.
On the island of Siquijor, lamp posts are typically painted yellow with black stripes at the bottom.
Images and statues of ancient Roman soldiers can be found on the island of Marinduque.
A black Street View car with a visible roof rack can be found in and around the city of General Santos.
In northwestern Bohol, you can find a Street View car with tape on the back.
An orange Street View car with visible side mirrors can be found on Corregidor Island.
A vehicle with several thick black bars can be found just south of the Mayon Volcano.
